claims.claim: Recurring default names ('Marcus Webb', 'Sarah Chen') and the number 47 appear across unrelated AI stories, alongside canon-breaking facts.
A character shifts from heated argument to gentleness with no organic transition.
Words like 'fluorescent', 'humming', 'particular' recur at rates traceable to a specific model's slop profile.
Literary agents receive near-identical AI query letters with the same voice, language and content even when the manuscripts look human.
claims.quote: almost identical query letters that used the same voice

claims.claim: An agent found the AI query offered no hook, fabricated a comp she never represented, and read as real-but-fake.
claims.quote: it appears real but it isn't

claims.feature: worse than a worst first draft
claims.claim: Larian's writing director rates generated dialogue 3/10 at best, below his own worst drafts, and says placeholder AI text does not help development.
claims.source: Adam Smith (Larian) via PC Gamer, Ted Litchfield
claims.quote: the results hit a 3/10 at best

claims.claim: Generated text across Grok, Claude and ChatGPT carries a recognizable smarmy, sycophantic tone that editing cannot remove cheaply.
claims.quote: a by turns smarmy and sycophantic tone

claims.claim: LLM NPCs pad trivial exchanges with unnecessary words and nonsensical attributes (eighteen as 'a heavy, beautiful number').
claims.quote: filling up space with completely unnecessary words

claims.claim: AI NPCs rephrase plain questions into stilted 'alive-sounding' forms, which reads as trying too hard.
claims.quote: How many years have you lived?

claims.claim: The same evaluative words ('heavy', 'beautiful', 'iconic', 'vibes') attach to age, names and shoe colour alike; conversations contain no actual meaning.
claims.quote: a full conversation that contains no actual meaning

claims.claim: The one thing that worked in Seed: creator-chosen personality types (curt vs gushing) read through the AI dialogue.
LLM NPCs in a Song-dynasty wuxia game discuss ketchup and accept fake pregnancies; players break canon at will.
claims.source: PC Gamer on Where Winds Meet
claims.quote: ketchup wasn't available during the Song dynasty

claims.claim: Nvidia's ACE demo NPC lines were structurally fine yet robotic, with no personality or charm.
An LLM NPC that forgets its faction or backstory, leaks modern facts into a fantasy setting, or spills quest secrets under manipulation is useless to a designer.
claims.source: Gameindustry.com, 'The Hard Problem of AI NPCs', 2026-05-18
claims.quote: forget their faction or personal backstory

claims.claim: Barks, journals and ambient NPC lines are the backbone of a game's sense of place; generic filler makes the whole world feel shallower.
claims.quote: disconnected, jilted, random stories to tell you

verdicts.trueWording: include Marcus, Marcus Webb, Sarah Chen, the last name Chen
verdicts.note: Author's-note tell list: 'Marcus Webb, Sarah Chen' is verbatim and contiguous. Same bullet adds "Claude also generates '47' for many random numbers -- times will sometimes end with :47" and "forget or confuse canon names"; a separate 'Incorrect canon details' bullet covers the rest. Every element of the claim is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: Whitney, with startling gentleness for someone who'd been arguing about tea infusion times ninety seconds earlier
verdicts.note: Appears twice: in the AI-generated sample fic posted by Flyg0n, and re-quoted in a 'Flyg0n said:' blockquote whose reader commentary makes the whiplash point -- 'She was getting so heated over boiling or steeping tea... that I thought she was an inherently terrifying and cruel person.' Attribution to Flyg0n is correct.

verdicts.trueWording: over-represented lexical patterns in LLM outputs
verdicts.note: ADVERSARIAL DOWNGRADE. 'heart pounding chest' IS verbatim on the repo page, but only as a throwaway illustration of what a trigram is: 'Trigrams (three-word combinations not including stop-words, e.g., heart pounding chest)'. The three words the claim names -- fluorescent, humming, particular -- appear ZERO times on the GitHub page; they come from the Thousand Roads thread's sample text (fluorescent x8, humming x4 there). The repo supports only the mechanism half: 'Analyze a model's outputs for repetitive words, bigrams, trigrams... and slop scores' and 'Cluster models based on slop profile similarity'. The quote does not evidence the claim attached to it.

verdicts.trueWording: she'd started to receive almost identical query letters that used the same voice, language and content
verdicts.note: Verbatim. The 'even when manuscripts look human' half is explicit: 'this was happening even when the manuscripts/illustrations being submitted appeared to be 100% made by humans.' Byline Naomi Jones and James Jones, Mar 09, 2026 -- matches. The post is partly paywalled but the quoted passage sits above the paywall.

verdicts.trueWording: It's called the uncanny valley for a reason: it appears real but it isn't
verdicts.note: Verbatim (curly apostrophe on the page). All three sub-claims confirmed: 'it did comp me to a writer I'd never heard of, let alone represented'; 'What it failed to do was provide any kind of hook for the book'; and the uncanny-valley framing. Kate Nash, Feb 23, 2026 -- matches.

verdicts.trueWording: the results hit a 3/10 at best
verdicts.note: Verbatim inside Adam Smith's quoted Reddit comment. 'Even my worst first drafts -- and there are a LOT of them -- are at least a 4/10' confirms 'below his own worst drafts'; "'how does generated placeholder text benefit development over simple stub text' -- it doesn't" confirms the placeholder half. The body calls him writing director; the headline says head writer. Ted Litchfield, 10 January 2026.

verdicts.trueWording: a by turns smarmy and sycophantic tone that I find utterly repulsive
verdicts.note: Verbatim, and it is Litchfield's own aside rather than Smith's: 'Whether it's Grok, Claude, or ChatGPT, people can never seem to get the genAI stink off'. The editing-cost half is the next sentence: 'At a certain point, editing bad writing is just more work than starting from scratch.'

verdicts.trueWording: the practice of filling up space with completely unnecessary words
verdicts.note: Verbatim. The eighteen example is on the page: "you don't need to then give the age of eighteen a bunch of nonsensical attributes, such as that it's a 'heavy, beautiful number'". Christopher Livingston, published 24 July 2026 -- date matches.

verdicts.trueWording: 'How many years have you lived?' is also another indication of an AI that's trying way too hard
verdicts.note: Verbatim, twice -- once as seedling dialogue, once in the critique. The 'alive-sounding' framing is explicit: 'You don't have to rephrase simple questions to sound alive!'

verdicts.trueWording: not as shallow as a full conversation that contains no actual meaning
verdicts.note: Verbatim. The vibe-adjective list is on the page: "'heavy' and 'beautiful' and 'iconic' and 'vibes' are words that come up constantly in Seed: not only is my seedling's age 'heavy' and 'beautiful' but so is my seedling's name and the color of someone's shoes (brown)".

verdicts.trueWording: Some speak very curtly, indicating they're not really interested in a conversation at all
verdicts.note: Verbatim, framed exactly as the claim's concession: 'I'll say this much: the Seedlings do at least have detectable personality types that come from players' choices during character creation, and those come through in how the AI talks'; the gushing counterpart follows in the same sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: ketchup wasn't available during the Song dynasty. Tomatoes weren't known in China back then.
verdicts.note: Verbatim (curly apostrophes on the page), spoken by NPC Zhao Dali. The fake-pregnancy half is the article's own subhead quote: 'I made him think that my character was pregnant with his child, then I demanded child support...'. Justin Wagner, 16 November 2025.

verdicts.trueWording: they're undeniably robotic, not offering any sort of personality or charm
verdicts.note: Verbatim. The 'structurally fine' half immediately precedes it: "Jin's responses are functionally sound; there's nothing inherently wrong with them in terms of structure or grammar." It is the Nvidia/Convai demo (Riva, NeMo, Audio2Face) in a cyberpunk ramen diner; the page does not use the brand name 'ACE'. Bradly Shankar, May 29, 2023 -- matches.

verdicts.trueWording: becomes completely useless to a game designer if they suddenly forget their faction or personal backstory
verdicts.note: Verbatim. All three failure modes are on the page: faction/backstory amnesia; 'A character must not reveal the main secrets of the final quest after a couple of leading or blatantly manipulative phrases'; and 'revealing modern facts in a fantasy or futuristic setting'. Bylined 'Special to GiN', May 18, 2026 -- date matches.

verdicts.trueWording: AI-generated NPCs with disconnected, jilted, random stories to tell you
verdicts.note: Verbatim. The backbone wording is explicit: 'Combat barks can characterise an enemy faction, journal entries can flesh out a culture' and 'they're the backbone on which the rest of' the script rests; plus 'causes Starfield to feel shallower as a result'. Harvey Randall, published 15 August 2026.
